subject: Communication
title: Kennedy's Inaugural Challenge
description: A short lesson to help you apply Kennedy's Inaugural Challenge.

hook.text: On January 20, 1961, JFK delivered one line that redefined the relationship between citizen and country.

buildup.text: Cold War tensions were peaking. The youngest elected president needed to project strength and vision.

discovery.text: 'Ask not what your country can do for you — ask what you can do for your country.' Antithesis perfected.

twist.text: The line uses antimetabole — reversing words for emphasis. It sounds profound because of its structure.

climax.text: Speechwriter Ted Sorensen crafted it, but JFK's delivery — clipped, Boston-accented — made it iconic.

punchline.text: A reversed sentence became America's marching orders.

quiz.question: What rhetorical device did JFK's famous 'Ask not' line use?

details.summary: John F. Kennedy's 1961 inaugural address, with its famous line 'Ask not what your country can do for you,' used antithesis, brevity, and aspirational language to unite a divided nation. Speechwriter Ted Sorensen crafted sentences designed to be quoted and remembered.
details.whyItMatters: Kennedy's speech demonstrates how deliberate rhetorical construction creates lines that outlive the speaker. Great speeches are engineered, not accidental.
takeaways: Antithesis flips phrases for memorable impact
The speech was deliberately crafted for quotability
Kennedy's delivery matched the precision of the text

faq.question: What is antithesis and why is it so effective?
faq.answer: Antithesis places contrasting ideas in parallel structure: ask not what your country can do for you, ask what you can do for your country. The reversal creates surprise, clarity, and memorability. The brain remembers contrasts because they create cognitive tension and resolution.

faq.question: How much did Ted Sorensen contribute to the speech?
faq.answer: Sorensen drafted most of the text, though Kennedy provided the vision and edited extensively. The ask not line has disputed origins, with echoes in earlier speeches by others. What matters is that the collaboration produced language that transcended both individuals.
